source: Adapted revision checklist based on VCAA's VCE Media Study Design, Units 3 and 4. Set texts differ between schools, so the narrative checkpoints are skills-based and should be applied to the texts you are studying. Checklist numbers are internal tracker IDs.
practiceNote: These practice questions and marking guides are original revision exercises, not VCAA examination questions. Regulatory bodies and classification rules change, so check current detail before relying on it.
papers: Use the VCAA examination specifications, past examinations and examination reports for official assessment resources.

points.area: Media codes and conventions
points.title: Technical codes
points.detail: Camera framing, angle and movement, lens choice, editing, lighting and sound, and the meaning each construction produces.

questions.q: Explain the effect of a high angle shot, shallow depth of field and a rapid cutting rate.
answer: A high angle shot looks down on the subject, diminishing them and positioning the audience to read them as vulnerable or powerless.
Shallow depth of field isolates the subject against a blurred background, directing attention and often suggesting subjective focus or emotional isolation.
A rapid cutting rate increases pace and tension, giving the audience less time to process each image.
Each is a construction rather than a neutral record, so the analysis must explain the effect rather than simply name the technique.

card.title: Technical codes
back: Camera framing, angle and movement, lens choice, editing, lighting and sound, and the meaning each construction produces.

points.area: Media codes and conventions
points.title: Symbolic codes
points.detail: Mise en scene including setting, costume, props, casting, performance and colour, and the cultural meanings these carry.

questions.q: Define mise en scene and explain how two of its components construct meaning.
answer: Mise en scene refers to everything arranged within the frame, including setting, costume, props, lighting, colour and performance.
Costume communicates character status, era, allegiance and personality before any dialogue is spoken.
Setting establishes not only place and time but also mood and the social world the character inhabits.
Because every element is deliberately chosen, each carries meaning the audience decodes using cultural knowledge.

card.title: Symbolic codes
back: Mise en scene including setting, costume, props, casting, performance and colour, and the cultural meanings these carry.

points.area: Media codes and conventions
points.title: Written and audio codes
points.detail: Titles, captions, dialogue, voiceover and on-screen text; diegetic and non-diegetic sound, score, silence and sound bridges.

questions.q: Distinguish between diegetic and non-diegetic sound and explain the effect of a non-diegetic score.
answer: Diegetic sound originates within the world of the story and can be heard by the characters, such as dialogue, footsteps or a car radio.
Non-diegetic sound is added for the audience and does not exist in the story world, such as an orchestral score or a voiceover narrator.
A non-diegetic score guides emotional response, cueing the audience how to feel about events before they are resolved.
It can also create irony when the music contradicts the action on screen, producing a critical rather than immersive response.

card.title: Written and audio codes
back: Titles, captions, dialogue, voiceover and on-screen text; diegetic and non-diegetic sound, score, silence and sound bridges.

points.area: Media codes and conventions
points.title: Genre conventions
points.detail: The recognisable patterns of setting, character type, narrative structure and iconography that define a genre, and the effect of subverting them.

questions.q: Explain how genre conventions shape audience expectation and the effect of subverting them.
answer: Conventions are repeated elements the audience recognises from previous texts in the genre, including iconography, character types and narrative patterns.
Recognition creates expectation, so the audience predicts how events will unfold and understands the text more quickly.
Subverting a convention denies the expected outcome, which can shock, create humour or force the audience to reconsider the genre's assumptions.
Subversion only works where the convention is well established, since the effect depends on the audience's prior knowledge.

card.title: Genre conventions
back: The recognisable patterns of setting, character type, narrative structure and iconography that define a genre, and the effect of subverting them.

points.area: Media codes and conventions
points.title: Media forms and their conventions
points.detail: The distinct conventions of film, television, photography, print, radio, podcast, games and online media, and the way form shapes content.

questions.q: Explain how the conventions of a podcast differ from those of a television documentary on the same subject.
answer: A podcast relies entirely on audio codes, so setting, evidence and emotion must be conveyed through voice, sound design, music and silence.
It commonly uses a conversational, first-person mode of address that creates intimacy with a listener who is often alone.
A television documentary can use visual evidence, archival footage and on-screen text alongside audio.
Consumption context also differs, since a podcast is often heard while doing something else, which affects pacing and the need for verbal signposting.

card.title: Media forms and their conventions
back: The distinct conventions of film, television, photography, print, radio, podcast, games and online media, and the way form shapes content.

points.area: Unit 3: Media narratives, contexts and pre-production — AoS 1: Narratives and their contexts
points.title: Narrative structure
points.detail: Linear and non-linear structure, exposition, complication, climax and resolution, and the effect of withholding or reordering information.

questions.q: Explain the effect of a non-linear narrative structure on the audience.
answer: A non-linear structure presents events out of chronological order, so the audience must actively assemble the story.
Withholding information creates suspense and can produce a reinterpretation of earlier scenes once context arrives.
Beginning at the end changes the question from what happens to how and why it happened, shifting emphasis to character and cause.
The structure itself carries meaning, so the analysis should explain why the maker ordered events this way.

card.title: Narrative structure
back: Linear and non-linear structure, exposition, complication, climax and resolution, and the effect of withholding or reordering information.

points.area: Unit 3: Media narratives, contexts and pre-production — AoS 1: Narratives and their contexts
points.title: Character and point of view
points.detail: Protagonist and antagonist construction, character arcs, alignment and allegiance, and the way narration positions the audience.

questions.q: Distinguish between audience alignment and audience allegiance with a character.
answer: Alignment concerns access: whose actions the audience follows and whose knowledge and interiority they share.
Allegiance concerns moral evaluation: whether the audience sympathises with the character and wants them to succeed.
A text can align the audience with a character while withholding allegiance, producing discomfort or critical distance.
Techniques including point of view shots, screen time, close-ups and voiceover build alignment, while the character's actions and treatment by the narrative shape allegiance.

card.title: Character and point of view
back: Protagonist and antagonist construction, character arcs, alignment and allegiance, and the way narration positions the audience.

points.area: Unit 3: Media narratives, contexts and pre-production — AoS 1: Narratives and their contexts
points.title: Setting, time and space
points.detail: The construction of story world and the manipulation of screen time and story time through duration, ellipsis and repetition.

questions.q: Explain how a montage sequence manipulates time and what it allows a narrative to achieve.
answer: A montage compresses a long period of story time into a short passage of screen time through a rapid succession of images.
It allows the narrative to convey development, such as training, a relationship forming or a business growing, without devoting scenes to each stage.
The selection of images within the montage also shapes interpretation by determining which moments of that period the audience sees.

card.title: Setting, time and space
back: The construction of story world and the manipulation of screen time and story time through duration, ellipsis and repetition.

points.area: Unit 3: Media narratives, contexts and pre-production — AoS 1: Narratives and their contexts
points.title: Representation
points.detail: The construction of groups, places and issues in media texts, and the selection, omission and framing that produce a representation.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by representation and why it is described as a construction rather than a reflection.
answer: A representation is the way a media text depicts a person, group, place, event or issue.
It is constructed through selection of what to include, omission of what to leave out, and framing of how the included material is presented.
Every representation therefore reflects choices made by its producers rather than reproducing reality neutrally.
Repeated representations across many texts shape what audiences come to regard as normal or typical, which is why they carry ideological significance.

card.title: Representation
back: The construction of groups, places and issues in media texts, and the selection, omission and framing that produce a representation.

points.area: Unit 3: Media narratives, contexts and pre-production — AoS 1: Narratives and their contexts
points.title: Ideology in media texts
points.detail: The values, beliefs and assumptions a text endorses or challenges, and the way narrative resolution reveals the text's position.

questions.q: Explain how the resolution of a narrative reveals the ideology of a text.
answer: The resolution determines which characters are rewarded and which are punished, which functions as the narrative's judgement.
The behaviours and values associated with the rewarded characters are therefore endorsed by the text.
Which conflicts are resolved and which are left unaddressed also indicates what the text treats as important.
An ambiguous or unresolved ending can itself be ideological, refusing the reassurance that a conventional resolution provides.

card.title: Ideology in media texts
back: The values, beliefs and assumptions a text endorses or challenges, and the way narrative resolution reveals the text's position.

points.area: Unit 3: Media narratives, contexts and pre-production — AoS 1: Narratives and their contexts
points.title: Production context and its influence
points.detail: How institutional, economic, cultural, historical and technological contexts shape the narratives that are made and how they are told.

questions.q: Explain how production context influences the narrative a media text presents.
answer: Economic context determines budget, which affects what can be filmed, the casting and the length of the production schedule.
Institutional context determines the commissioning body's requirements, including target audience, classification and running time.
Cultural and historical context shapes which stories are considered worth telling and which representations are acceptable at that time.
Technological context determines available techniques, so what is possible in production and distribution shapes narrative form.

card.title: Production context and its influence
back: How institutional, economic, cultural, historical and technological contexts shape the narratives that are made and how they are told.

points.area: Unit 3: Media narratives, contexts and pre-production — AoS 1: Narratives and their contexts
points.title: Audience reception context
points.detail: How the audience's own social, cultural and historical position shapes their reading of a text, and why readings differ over time.

questions.q: Explain why the same media text can be read differently by two audiences.
answer: Audiences bring their own cultural knowledge, values and experience to a text, and these shape which meanings they make.
A representation that appeared unremarkable to its original audience may read as offensive to a later one whose values have changed.
Reception context also includes where and how the text is consumed, since viewing in a cinema differs from viewing on a phone.
Meaning is therefore produced in the interaction between text and audience rather than residing solely in the text.

card.title: Audience reception context
back: How the audience's own social, cultural and historical position shapes their reading of a text, and why readings differ over time.

points.area: Unit 3: Media narratives, contexts and pre-production — AoS 2: Research, development and experimentation
points.title: Developing a production concept
points.detail: Generating and testing ideas, defining the intended audience, form and purpose, and researching comparable works.

questions.q: Explain what must be established before production design begins.
answer: The media form and the specific product to be made, since each form has its own conventions and technical requirements.
The intended audience, defined specifically rather than as a general public, since audience determines style, content and platform.
The purpose of the production, whether to entertain, inform, persuade or provoke, which shapes every subsequent decision.
Research into comparable works establishes the conventions the audience will expect and identifies opportunities for distinction.

card.title: Developing a production concept
back: Generating and testing ideas, defining the intended audience, form and purpose, and researching comparable works.

points.area: Unit 3: Media narratives, contexts and pre-production — AoS 3: Pre-production planning
points.title: The production design plan
points.detail: Documenting the intentions, form, audience, style and technical specifications of the production so it can be realised.

questions.q: State what a production design plan must specify and why detail matters.
answer: The intended form, audience, purpose and style, including references that establish the visual and aural approach.
Technical specifications such as shot lists, locations, cast, equipment, aspect ratio and duration.
A schedule and resource list covering what must be arranged before production begins.
Detail matters because decisions deferred to the shoot are made under time pressure and usually produce a weaker result.

card.title: The production design plan
back: Documenting the intentions, form, audience, style and technical specifications of the production so it can be realised.

points.area: Unit 3: Media narratives, contexts and pre-production — AoS 3: Pre-production planning
points.title: Storyboards, scripts and shot lists
points.detail: Planning documents that specify framing, movement, sound, dialogue and sequence before production.

questions.q: Explain what a storyboard communicates and how it differs from a script.
answer: A storyboard visualises each shot, specifying framing, angle, camera movement and the arrangement of subjects within the frame.
It usually includes notes on duration, transitions and accompanying sound.
A script specifies dialogue, action and sound in written form but does not fix the visual treatment.
The storyboard therefore translates the script into the visual language of the chosen form and allows problems to be identified before shooting.

card.title: Storyboards, scripts and shot lists
back: Planning documents that specify framing, movement, sound, dialogue and sequence before production.

points.area: Unit 3: Media narratives, contexts and pre-production — AoS 3: Pre-production planning
points.title: Pre-production planning and logistics
points.detail: Scheduling, location scouting, casting, equipment, permissions, risk assessment and contingency planning.

questions.q: Name four pre-production tasks and explain why contingency planning matters.
answer: Location scouting to confirm access, light, sound conditions and power availability.
Casting and crew arrangement, and booking equipment for the required dates.
Obtaining permissions and releases for locations, participants and any copyright material used.
Contingency planning matters because weather, illness and equipment failure are routine, and a production without alternatives loses the shoot day entirely.

card.title: Pre-production planning and logistics
back: Scheduling, location scouting, casting, equipment, permissions, risk assessment and contingency planning.

points.area: Unit 4: Media production; agency and control in and of the media — AoS 1: Media production
points.title: Production
points.detail: Realising the design plan through filming, recording, photographing or authoring, and managing the trade-off between plan and circumstance.

questions.q: Explain how a producer should respond when conditions on the day make part of the design plan impossible.
answer: Identify what the shot or element was intended to communicate, since the purpose matters more than the specific execution.
Devise an alternative that serves the same narrative or communicative function within the available conditions.
Document the change and its reason, so the evaluation can assess the finished work against the revised intention.

card.title: Production
back: Realising the design plan through filming, recording, photographing or authoring, and managing the trade-off between plan and circumstance.

points.area: Unit 4: Media production; agency and control in and of the media — AoS 1: Media production
points.title: Post-production
points.detail: Editing for continuity, pace and meaning, colour grading, sound mixing, titles and the export specifications for the chosen platform.

questions.q: Explain how editing constructs meaning, referring to two specific editing decisions.
answer: Editing determines the order in which the audience receives information, so meaning is created in the juxtaposition of shots rather than within either shot alone.
Shot duration controls pace and attention: holding on a reaction gives it weight, while cutting away denies it.
A cut between two unrelated images invites the audience to infer a relationship between them, which is how montage generates meaning.
Transitions, sound bridges and continuity decisions also shape whether the audience experiences the sequence as continuous or fragmented.

card.title: Post-production
back: Editing for continuity, pace and meaning, colour grading, sound mixing, titles and the export specifications for the chosen platform.

points.area: Unit 4: Media production; agency and control in and of the media — AoS 1: Media production
points.title: Realising the intended style
points.detail: Ensuring technical and symbolic codes are consistent with the design plan and appropriate to the form, audience and purpose.

questions.q: Explain what it means for a production to have a consistent style and why inconsistency weakens a work.
answer: Consistency means the technical and symbolic codes work together throughout, so lighting, colour, framing, editing pace and sound share a coherent approach.
A consistent style creates a unified world that the audience accepts and becomes absorbed in.
Inconsistency draws attention to the construction itself, breaking absorption and reading as a technical error rather than a deliberate choice.

card.title: Realising the intended style
back: Ensuring technical and symbolic codes are consistent with the design plan and appropriate to the form, audience and purpose.

points.area: Unit 4: Media production; agency and control in and of the media — AoS 1: Media production
points.title: Evaluating the finished production
points.detail: Assessing the product against the intentions in the design plan, with evidence from the work itself and from audience response.

questions.q: Explain how to evaluate a media production against its design plan.
answer: Address each stated intention separately: form, audience, purpose and style, rather than giving a general impression.
Point to specific moments in the finished work as evidence of whether each intention was realised.
Acknowledge where the outcome departed from the plan and assess whether the departure improved or weakened the work.
Include audience response where available, since the intended effect on an audience cannot be verified by the maker alone.

card.title: Evaluating the finished production
back: Assessing the product against the intentions in the design plan, with evidence from the work itself and from audience response.

points.area: Unit 4: Media production; agency and control in and of the media — AoS 2: Agency and control in the media
points.title: Media ownership and concentration
points.detail: Patterns of ownership, concentration of media ownership in Australia, and the influence of ownership on content and editorial direction.

questions.q: Explain why concentration of media ownership is regarded as a concern for public debate.
answer: Concentration means a small number of owners control the outlets through which most people receive news and commentary.
Owners influence content through editorial appointments, resourcing decisions and the issues their outlets choose to pursue.
A narrower range of owners tends to produce a narrower range of perspectives available to the public.
This matters for democratic debate, since citizens form political judgements using information supplied by these outlets.

card.title: Media ownership and concentration
back: Patterns of ownership, concentration of media ownership in Australia, and the influence of ownership on content and editorial direction.

points.area: Unit 4: Media production; agency and control in and of the media — AoS 2: Agency and control in the media
points.title: Commercial influences on content
points.detail: Advertising revenue, sponsorship, ratings and clicks, and the effect of commercial pressure on what is produced and published.

questions.q: Explain how the need for advertising revenue influences media content.
answer: Content must attract and retain the audience that advertisers wish to reach, so material appealing to that demographic is prioritised.
Online, revenue tied to clicks and attention rewards content that provokes strong immediate reaction, which favours conflict and sensation.
Advertisers may withdraw from outlets publishing material they consider damaging to their brand, creating indirect pressure on editorial choices.
Expensive investigative work that serves few readers is difficult to sustain on a commercial model, which affects the type of journalism produced.

card.title: Commercial influences on content
back: Advertising revenue, sponsorship, ratings and clicks, and the effect of commercial pressure on what is produced and published.

points.area: Unit 4: Media production; agency and control in and of the media — AoS 2: Agency and control in the media
points.title: Regulation and classification
points.detail: Classification of films, television and games, industry codes of practice, complaints processes and the differing regulation of broadcast and online media.

questions.q: Explain the purposes of media classification and why online content is harder to regulate than broadcast.
answer: Classification informs audiences about content so they can make decisions, and restricts access to some material by age.
It balances the protection of children and community standards against freedom of expression and the interests of producers.
Broadcast media operate under licences within one jurisdiction, so regulators can impose conditions and penalties on identifiable licence holders.
Online content is produced globally, distributed by platforms outside national jurisdiction and published continuously in enormous volume, so pre-publication classification is impractical.

card.title: Regulation and classification
back: Classification of films, television and games, industry codes of practice, complaints processes and the differing regulation of broadcast and online media.

points.area: Unit 4: Media production; agency and control in and of the media — AoS 2: Agency and control in the media
points.title: Codes of practice and journalistic ethics
points.detail: Accuracy, fairness, privacy, the distinction between news and comment, and the handling of complaints and corrections.

questions.q: Explain four principles commonly found in journalistic codes of practice.
answer: Accuracy: reporting should be factually correct and verified, with errors corrected promptly and prominently.
Fairness: those criticised should be given an opportunity to respond, and reporting should not be misleading through selective omission.
Distinction between news and comment: opinion should be clearly identified so audiences know which they are reading.
Privacy: intrusion requires justification in the public interest, which is not the same as what the public finds interesting.

card.title: Codes of practice and journalistic ethics
card.front: Codes of practice and journalistic ethics
back: Accuracy, fairness, privacy, the distinction between news and comment, and the handling of complaints and corrections.

points.area: Unit 4: Media production; agency and control in and of the media — AoS 2: Agency and control in the media
points.title: Platforms, algorithms and gatekeeping
points.detail: The shift of gatekeeping from editors to algorithms, personalisation, filter effects and the accountability of platforms for content.

questions.q: Explain how algorithmic curation differs from traditional editorial gatekeeping, and one consequence.
answer: Traditional gatekeeping involved editors deciding what to publish and in what prominence, applying professional judgement for which they were accountable.
Algorithmic curation selects and ranks content automatically for each user based on predicted engagement.
The criteria are commercial and largely opaque, and no individual takes editorial responsibility for the resulting selection.
A consequence is that users receive personalised and differing versions of events, which fragments the shared information base on which public debate depends.

card.title: Platforms, algorithms and gatekeeping
back: The shift of gatekeeping from editors to algorithms, personalisation, filter effects and the accountability of platforms for content.

points.area: Unit 4: Media production; agency and control in and of the media — AoS 2: Agency and control in the media
points.title: Audience agency and user-generated content
points.detail: The shift from audiences as receivers to audiences as producers and distributors, and the consequences for control over media.

questions.q: Explain how audiences have gained agency in the contemporary media landscape, and one limitation on that agency.
answer: Low-cost production tools and open distribution platforms allow individuals to produce and publish media without institutional approval.
Audiences also curate, comment on, remix and redistribute content, so they participate in circulation rather than only receiving it.
This allows perspectives excluded by mainstream outlets to reach substantial audiences directly.
The limitation is that visibility remains controlled by platform algorithms owned by a few corporations, so reaching an audience still depends on decisions made elsewhere.

card.title: Audience agency and user-generated content
back: The shift from audiences as receivers to audiences as producers and distributors, and the consequences for control over media.

points.area: Unit 4: Media production; agency and control in and of the media — AoS 2: Agency and control in the media
points.title: Misinformation and trust
points.detail: The spread of false information, the economics that reward it, and the effects on trust in media institutions.

questions.q: Explain why misinformation spreads effectively on social platforms.
answer: Platform algorithms promote content that generates engagement, and false or sensational claims often provoke stronger reactions than accurate ones.
There is no pre-publication verification, so a claim can reach a large audience before any correction is possible.
Corrections reach far fewer people than the original claim and rarely undo the initial impression.
Personalisation means users encounter claims within networks of people who already agree, which increases their apparent credibility.

card.title: Misinformation and trust
back: The spread of false information, the economics that reward it, and the effects on trust in media institutions.

points.area: Audience theory and media influence
points.title: Hypodermic needle model
points.detail: The early view of audiences as passive recipients into whom messages are directly injected, and the criticisms of this model.

questions.q: Explain the hypodermic needle model and two criticisms of it.
answer: The model proposes that media messages are injected directly into a passive audience, producing uniform and immediate effects.
It emerged in an era of concern about propaganda and mass broadcast media reaching large undifferentiated audiences.
It is criticised for treating audiences as uniform, ignoring the differences in interpretation that people bring to a text.
It is also criticised for assuming a direct causal effect that empirical research has not demonstrated, and for ignoring social context and interpersonal influence.

card.title: Hypodermic needle model
back: The early view of audiences as passive recipients into whom messages are directly injected, and the criticisms of this model.

points.area: Audience theory and media influence
points.title: Two-step flow and opinion leaders
points.detail: The role of opinion leaders in mediating media messages within social networks, and the influence of interpersonal communication.

questions.q: Explain the two-step flow model and how it revised earlier views of media influence.
answer: The model proposes that media messages reach opinion leaders first, who interpret them and pass them on within their social networks.
Influence therefore operates through personal relationships as well as through direct exposure to media.
It revised earlier views by showing that social context mediates media effects, so the audience is not a mass of isolated individuals.

card.title: Two-step flow and opinion leaders
back: The role of opinion leaders in mediating media messages within social networks, and the influence of interpersonal communication.

points.area: Audience theory and media influence
points.title: Uses and gratifications
points.detail: The active audience selecting media to satisfy needs for information, personal identity, social interaction and entertainment.

questions.q: Explain the uses and gratifications approach and how it reverses the question asked by earlier theories.
answer: The approach proposes that audiences actively select media to satisfy their own needs rather than passively receiving whatever is transmitted.
Identified gratifications include information and surveillance, personal identity, social interaction and integration, and entertainment or escape.
It reverses the question from what media do to people, to what people do with media.
A criticism is that it can overstate audience freedom, since the available choices are determined by producers and platforms.

card.title: Uses and gratifications
back: The active audience selecting media to satisfy needs for information, personal identity, social interaction and entertainment.

points.area: Audience theory and media influence
points.title: Reception theory and reading positions
points.detail: Dominant, negotiated and oppositional readings, and the encoding of a preferred meaning that audiences may or may not accept.

questions.q: Explain the three reading positions in reception theory with an example.
answer: A dominant or preferred reading accepts the meaning the producers encoded into the text.
A negotiated reading accepts the overall framework but resists or modifies parts of it based on the viewer's own circumstances.
An oppositional reading understands the preferred meaning but rejects it, reading the text against its intended position.
An advertisement promoting a product as essential may be accepted, partly accepted as appealing but unaffordable, or rejected as manipulative marketing.

card.title: Reception theory and reading positions
back: Dominant, negotiated and oppositional readings, and the encoding of a preferred meaning that audiences may or may not accept.

points.area: Audience theory and media influence
points.title: Cultivation theory
points.detail: The proposition that long-term cumulative exposure shapes perception of reality, including mean world syndrome, and the limits of the evidence.

questions.q: Explain cultivation theory and one strength and one limitation of it.
answer: Cultivation theory proposes that heavy long-term exposure to consistent media representations gradually shapes a person's perception of social reality.
Mean world syndrome describes heavy viewers of violent content overestimating the level of danger in their society.
A strength is that it addresses cumulative long-term influence rather than immediate effects, which better matches how media is actually consumed.
A limitation is that correlation between heavy viewing and fearful perception does not establish direction of causation, since anxious people may choose such content.

card.title: Cultivation theory
back: The proposition that long-term cumulative exposure shapes perception of reality, including mean world syndrome, and the limits of the evidence.

points.area: Audience theory and media influence
points.title: Debates about media influence
points.detail: Weighing evidence about media effects, the role of moral panic, and the difficulty of isolating media influence from other social factors.

questions.q: Explain why it is difficult to establish that media consumption causes a particular behaviour.
answer: Media consumption occurs alongside many other influences including family, peers, economic circumstances and education, which are difficult to separate.
Correlational studies cannot establish direction, since a predisposition may cause both the media choice and the behaviour.
Laboratory experiments can demonstrate short-term effects but cannot replicate long-term real-world consumption.
Public debate is often driven by moral panic following a specific incident, which produces conclusions unsupported by the weight of research.

card.title: Debates about media influence
back: Weighing evidence about media effects, the role of moral panic, and the difficulty of isolating media influence from other social factors.

points.area: Exam technique
points.title: Analysing an unseen text
points.detail: Identifying form, purpose and audience, naming specific codes, and explaining the meaning each construction produces.

questions.q: Explain the structure of a strong response analysing an unseen media text.
answer: Identify the media form, its likely purpose and its intended audience from evidence in the text.
Identify specific technical and symbolic codes, naming them precisely rather than describing the content generally.
Explain the meaning each code constructs and how the audience is positioned by it.
Connect the observations to an overall reading of what the text communicates and to whom.

card.title: Analysing an unseen text
back: Identifying form, purpose and audience, naming specific codes, and explaining the meaning each construction produces.

points.area: Exam technique
points.title: Using examples from set texts
points.detail: Recalling specific moments, shots and sequences with enough precision to serve as evidence, rather than summarising plot.

questions.q: Explain what makes an example from a set text strong evidence in a Media response.
answer: It refers to a specific moment, shot or sequence rather than to the text in general or to its plot as a whole.
It names the codes at work in that moment, such as the framing, lighting, sound or editing.
It explains what that specific construction communicates, which is what earns the analysis marks.

card.title: Using examples from set texts
back: Recalling specific moments, shots and sequences with enough precision to serve as evidence, rather than summarising plot.

points.area: Exam technique
points.title: Command terms and media terminology
points.detail: Matching response depth to the command term, and using precise media terminology rather than everyday description.

questions.q: Name three imprecise phrases common in Media responses and give the precise alternative for each.
answer: 'The camera zooms in' is often used for what is actually a cut to a closer shot or a dolly in; name the actual technique.
'Sad music plays' should specify that a non-diegetic score in a minor key positions the audience to read the scene as melancholy.
'It shows that' should be replaced with a verb describing the construction, such as 'the low key lighting constructs the character as threatening'.

card.title: Command terms and media terminology
back: Matching response depth to the command term, and using precise media terminology rather than everyday description.
